A two-dimensional example.

A Worked Example of the Proof of KLS Conjecture

This worked example accompanies “A Dimension-Free Bound on the Poincaré Constant of Isotropic Log-Concave Measures”, by Krishnakumar Balasubramanian and Shiva Kasiviswanathan.

Here, we consider a two-dimensional example that makes the ingredients of the paper’s argument concrete. We work through its calculations below and identify the general results we use from the paper by name and number. This companion illustrates the proposed argument; it does not independently verify the paper’s general theorems.

The Poincaré inequality compares the variance of a function with the average squared size of its gradient:

Var⁡μf≤KP Eμ∣∇f∣2.\Var_\mu f\le K_{\mathrm{P}}\,\E_\mu|\nabla f|^2.Varμ​f≤KP​Eμ​∣∇f∣2.

The left side measures how much a function fluctuates. The right side measures how much it changes locally. Recovering a centered function from its gradient is therefore exactly the operation we need to control. The gradient determines the function up to an additive constant, which the mean-zero condition fixes. For a centered function, variance is the average of its square, so the Poincaré inequality asks us to bound that average by a constant times the average squared gradient. The challenge is to control this recovery for every admissible gradient, starting from estimates for polynomials.

From the Paper · Compatible-Tensor Hodge Estimate

Lemma 3.1 extends the curvature bound to every tensor rank. It applies to regular laws: centered laws with a smooth potential whose Hessian is bounded above and below by positive multiples of the identity. If D2V⪰aIdD^2V\succeq a\IdD2V⪰aId, write Dm\mathscr D_mDm​ for differentiation on centered compatible rank-mmm fields. For every FFF in the domain of its adjoint, the lemma gives

∥Dm∗F∥22≥∥∇F∥22+a∥F∥22.\|\mathscr D_m^*F\|_2^2\ge\|\nabla F\|_2^2+a\|F\|_2^2.∥Dm∗​F∥22​≥∥∇F∥22​+a∥F∥22​.

The lower curvature bound aaa survives unchanged as the number of tensor indices grows. This uniformity is what lets the next step control arbitrarily long integration chains.

Uniform Bounds for Integration Powers

Appell norms observe integration chains that start at constant tensors. A general compatible input can depend on position in any square-integrable way. Curvature connects these special observations to the full integration operator.

The paper bundles all tensor ranks into one Hilbert space, so that a single operator J\mathsf JJ lowers rank and L\mathsf LL supplies the constant-input primitives. The inverse comparison in §4.2, based on Lemma 3.1, gives the following inequality. Appendix B supplies the operator-domain details.

J∗J⪯g(JJ∗+LL∗),g(u)=u1+au,∥Jj−1L∥≤cj(ν).\mathsf J^*\mathsf J\preceq g(\mathsf J\mathsf J^*+\mathsf L\mathsf L^*),\qquad g(u)=\frac{u}{1+au}, \qquad \|\mathsf J^{j-1}\mathsf L\|\le c_j(\nu).J∗J⪯g(JJ∗+LL∗),g(u)=1+auu​,∥Jj−1L∥≤cj​(ν).

The function ggg acts on the operator’s spectral values, just as a function of a symmetric matrix acts on its eigenvalues. Its denominator records the contribution of curvature. The uniform power lemma, Lemma 5.1, uses this comparison and finitely many constant-input bounds to control every power of J\mathsf JJ.

Stability Under Regular Approximation

The unnormalized densities satisfy e−Vε(x)≤e−3∣x∣e^{-V_\varepsilon(x)}\le e^{-\sqrt3|x|}e−Vε​(x)≤e−3​∣x∣ and converge pointwise to it. The majorant and all of its polynomial multiples are integrable. Dominated convergence therefore gives convergence of normalization, covariance and every fixed moment. For smooth compactly supported fff, the variance and gradient integral under the covariance-normalized laws converge to their counterparts under μ\muμ. Passing to the limit preserves the same constant. The approximation argument of §9 and Appendix F then extends the inequality to locally Lipschitz functions with finite gradient energy, as in Theorem 1.1.

The worked example exposes each role: compatibility allows integration; the Hodge estimate controls the cost of enforcing it; Appell polynomials record constant-input chains; the power lemma controls arbitrary chains; localization adds curvature; the moving coefficients preserve centering; reverse transfer closes the degree induction. Only after all degrees are available can the curvature dependence disappear.
